questions.question: Which of the following are both non-cellular pathogens?
questions.answer: Viruses (nucleic acid in a protein coat) and prions (misfolded proteins) are not made of cells. Bacteria and protozoa are cellular, so D.

questions.question: Mutations occurring in cells which do not go on to form gametes can be classified as:
questions.answer: Mutations in body (non-gamete-forming) cells are somatic mutations. They affect only that individual and are not inherited, whereas germ-line mutations occur in cells that form gametes.

questions.question: In the diagram, X represents a cell with the function of secreting chemicals that stimulate the cloning of B and T lymphocytes. What type of cell is X?
questions.answer: T helper cells (CD4) secrete cytokines that stimulate B cells to clone and differentiate into plasma cells and memory cells, and stimulate T killer cells to clone. Plasma cells make antibodies and memory cells store memory, so the answer is D.

questions.question:
The table shows the water gained and lost by two species of mammals.

| | Mammal A (mL/day) | Mammal A (% of total) | Mammal B (mL/day) | Mammal B (% of total) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Water gain** | | | | |
| drinking | 0 | 0 | 1500 | 60 |
| eating | 6 | 10 | 750 | 30 |
| metabolism | 54 | 90 | 250 | 10 |
| **Water loss** | | | | |
| evaporation | 43.9 | 73 | 900 | 36 |
| urine | 13.5 | 23 | 1500 | 60 |
| third avenue of water loss | 2.6 | 4 | 100 | 4 |

Which of the following statements is consistent with the given data?
options: The high proportion of water lost through evaporation in species A shows that species A is adapted to survive in a hot and dry climate.
The higher metabolic rate of species B compared to species A indicates that species B could be a desert animal.
0% water gain and 13.5 mL water loss through urine are indicators of mammal A being a hibernating animal.
The overall water gain and loss is higher for mammal B than mammal A, indicating that mammal B has larger surface area.
questions.answer:
Mammal A gains no water by drinking and gets 90% of its water from metabolism, with only 13.5 mL lost as urine, so it is adapted to a dry environment. Most of its (small) water loss is by evaporation, which is expected for an animal that conserves water by producing concentrated urine. The school's key gives A (it also accepted D). B is wrong because the table shows B's *metabolic water* is only 10% of its gain and B drinks heavily. C is wrong because a low urine output does not show hibernation. D is a possible-but-unsupported inference (the table gives no surface area).

*School note:* the marking guide lists the key as "A/D"; A is used here.

questions.question:
In 2014, during an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD) in West Africa, thousands of local people and several healthcare workers died. Infections resulted from human-to-human transmission through contact with broken skin, mucus, bodily fluids and secretions.

Which of the following measures could prevent future outbreaks of EVD?
questions.answer: Ebola is spread by direct contact with infected people, so isolating (quarantining) infected people stops transmission. Antibiotics do not work on viruses, and vaccination of already-infected people does not stop them being infectious. The school's key is B.

questions.question:
The hormones progesterone and luteinising hormone (LH) were measured in a woman's blood over 40 days, as shown in the graph. Four times (A–D) are marked with arrows at about day 8, day 13, day 21 and day 34.

When did her menstrual bleed start?
questions.answer: Menstruation begins when the corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone falls to a low level (and the uterine lining breaks down). Progesterone peaks around day 13–17 and has fallen to a low baseline by about day 21, so the bleed starts at C (day 21).

questions.question: The gel below shows the results of a DNA profile of a family (lanes: man, child I, child II, woman). What conclusion can be made from the analysis of these DNA fragments?
options: Both children are related to both parents.
Child I is related to the man but child II is not.
Both children are unrelated to either of the parents.
Child II is related to the man but child I is not.
questions.answer: Every band in each child's lane matches a band in either the man's or the woman's lane, so each child has inherited half of their DNA fragments from each parent: both children are related to both parents.

questions.question: The graph shows the relationship between body core temperature and environmental temperature of four different organisms (I–IV). Which of the following statements is best supported by the data?
options: Animals I and II are most likely mammals.
Animal II is endothermic over the environmental temperature range of 0 to 30 °C.
Animal III maintains its body core temperature relatively constant by shivering when the environmental temperature falls below 37 °C.
Animal IV is most likely a mammal in polar region.
questions.answer: Between 0 and 30 °C animal II keeps its core temperature almost constant (about 32–33 °C) despite the environmental temperature changing, so it is regulating its temperature using metabolic heat: it is endothermic. A is not supported (I and II could be birds or mammals), C is wrong because III's temperature follows the environment, and D is wrong because IV's temperature follows the environment, so it is an ectotherm.

questions.question:
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a genetic disorder in which the muscles waste away due to inadequate production of a protein called dystrophin. A group of researchers isolated the gene for dystrophin and inserted it into a plasmid extracted from a bacterium. A concentrated solution of these recombinant plasmids was then injected into the muscles of mice with a missense mutation in the gene for dystrophin.

Which of the following is the function of the injected plasmid in treating the disorder?
options: To stimulate a humoral immune response to the bacteria in the treated mice.
To deliver the dystrophin protein directly to the muscles of the treated mice.
To act as a vector for the delivery of dystrophin genes to the muscle cells of the treated mice.
To create a strain of genetically engineered bacteria that will cure Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
questions.answer: The recombinant plasmid acts as a vector carrying the functional dystrophin gene into the muscle cells, where the gene can be expressed. It delivers the gene, not the protein.

questions.question:
A pathology centre took blood samples from three patients. One patient was suspected of suffering from anaemia, which reduces the oxygen carrying capacity of the blood. Another patient was suffering from human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which attacks T cells. The third patient had a red, raised area following a puncture wound.

The table shows the numbers of different types of blood cells found in the blood samples (cells/mm³).

| Type of blood cell | Reference range (95% of healthy individuals) | Patient X | Patient Y | Patient Z |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phagocyte | 3000 – 8000 | 2689 | 9680 | 7370 |
| Lymphocyte | 800 – 5000 | 273 | 3741 | 2692 |
| Erythrocyte | 3 000 000 – 6 000 000 | 2 873 000 | 5 243 000 | 2 148 000 |

Which of the following correctly matches the patient to the condition?

| | Anaemia | HIV | Infected wound |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. | Y | X | Z |
| B. | X | Z | Y |
| C. | Z | Y | X |
| D. | Z | X | Y |
options: Anaemia: Y; HIV: X; Infected wound: Z
Anaemia: X; HIV: Z; Infected wound: Y
Anaemia: Z; HIV: Y; Infected wound: X
Anaemia: Z; HIV: X; Infected wound: Y
questions.answer: Anaemia means too few red blood cells: only Patient Z's erythrocyte count (2 148 000) is below the reference range, but note that Patient X's count (2 873 000) is also slightly low. HIV destroys T lymphocytes, so lymphocytes will be very low: Patient X (273, below 800). An infected wound causes a raised phagocyte count (above 8000): Patient Y (9680). So Z = anaemia, X = HIV, Y = infected wound: D.

questions.question:
Over millions of years of evolution, mutations occur at a broadly constant rate within a gene. This allows genes to be used as molecular clocks. The diagram shows how the base sequence in part of a gene changed as two evolutionary lineages diverged from an original base sequence (original CAATTTATCG; 5 million years after diverging, Species X has CAATTGATCG and Species Y has CGATTTATCG; 10 million years after diverging, Species X has CAATTGCTCG and Species Y has CGGTTTATCG).

Assuming this rate of mutation continued, by how many bases would this part of the gene differ in Species X compared with Species Y 20 million years after diverging from the original base sequence?
questions.answer: Each lineage gained one base change every 5 million years (compare the sequences at 0, 5 and 10 million years). After 20 million years each lineage will have accumulated 4 changes, so the two species can differ at up to $4+4=8$ bases (assuming no change hits the same position twice).

questions.question: Which of the following statements best explains why bacteria are used in gene cloning?
options: Bacteria can replicate non-bacterial sequences of DNA in a short time.
Bacteria allow the entry of foreign DNA into their nuclei.
Bacteria replicate exponentially by undergoing mitotic divisions.
Bacteria contain restriction enzymes that randomly cut chromosomes into fragments of varying size.
questions.answer: Bacteria reproduce rapidly and, once a recombinant plasmid has been taken up, copy the inserted foreign DNA each time the plasmid replicates. B is wrong (bacteria have no nucleus), C is wrong (bacteria divide by binary fission, not mitosis), and D is wrong (restriction enzymes cut at specific recognition sites, not randomly).

questions.question:
The diagram shows a bacterial plasmid with restriction sites for three different restriction endonucleases (Sal1 ×2, EcoR1 ×3, BamH1 ×1).

Which row in the table identifies the number of fragments produced if the plasmid was cut with the combinations of restriction endonucleases shown?

| | Sal1 and BamH1 | Sal1 and EcoR1 |
|---|---|---|
| A. | 3 | 4 |
| B. | 3 | 5 |
| C. | 4 | 4 |
| D. | 4 | 5 |
questions.answer: A circular plasmid cut at $n$ sites gives $n$ fragments. Sal1 and BamH1: $2+1=3$ cuts, so 3 fragments. Sal1 and EcoR1: $2+3=5$ cuts, so 5 fragments. Row B.

questions.question:
Consider the following steps taking place in the cell cycle:

I. Re-formation of nuclear membranes
II. Pairing of homologous chromosomes
III. DNA replication

Which of these take(s) place during either interphase or mitosis in animal cells?
questions.answer: I (telophase of mitosis) and III (S phase of interphase) occur. Pairing of homologous chromosomes (synapsis) occurs in prophase I of meiosis, not in mitosis or interphase.

questions.question:
Osmoregulation is the process by which water and salt (solute) concentration in the blood achieves homeostasis using aldosterone and anti-diuretic hormone (ADH).

Aldosterone acts on sodium ions causing them to be actively reabsorbed back into the blood from the kidney. As a result, the blood in the capillaries surrounding the kidney's distal tubule will have a higher solute concentration.

An increase in solute concentration in the blood causes the pituitary gland to secrete ADH into the blood stream to increase the permeability of distal tubules to water. This increases the amount of water reabsorbed back into the blood from the kidney. The amount of ADH secreted will decrease when the solute concentration in the blood returns to normal.

A dehydrated marathon runner consumed a concentrated salt sports drink to satisfy his thirst. How does his body control the two hormones, ADH and aldosterone, to help to re-establish normal water balance?
options: ADH is released and aldosterone is inhibited
ADH is inhibited and aldosterone is released
Both ADH and aldosterone are released
Both ADH and aldosterone are inhibited
questions.answer: The salt drink raises blood solute concentration, which stimulates ADH release so that more water is reabsorbed. Aldosterone would cause even more sodium to be reabsorbed and further raise the solute concentration, so its release is inhibited.

questions.question:
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is the hormone that stimulates cholesterol conversion to progesterone and testosterone. Progesterone is then converted to cortisol due to the action of an enzyme, 21-hydroxylase. If the enzyme is defective, the synthesis of cortisol is reduced, and an excess of testosterone is produced. This results in a disorder called congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH).

To diagnose CAH, an ACTH stimulation test is performed. Blood is measured for starting levels of testosterone. ACTH is then injected, and another blood sample is taken and analysed after 120 minutes.

Figure 1 shows the ACTH pathway (cortisol exerts negative feedback on the anterior pituitary, and the defective enzyme blocks progesterone → cortisol). White bars represent normal individuals and black bars represent CAH individuals. Using the key, which of the following graphs (A–D) best depicts the changes in the level of testosterone in an ACTH stimulation test?
questions.answer: In CAH, cortisol cannot be made, so there is no negative feedback to the pituitary: ACTH is high and the adrenal gland diverts more cholesterol and progesterone to testosterone. CAH individuals therefore have higher testosterone before the test, and injected ACTH raises it much further. Normal individuals show only a small change. This is graph A (black bars higher before, and markedly higher after).

questions.question:
A comet assay is a technique used to determine the amount of double-strand breakages in DNA (DNA damage) in cells. The DNA of a nucleus placed on an agarose gel is subjected to electrophoresis and stained. Undamaged DNA appears as a round shape (the head) and fragments of damaged DNA extend out from the head (the tail). The length of the tail corresponds to the amount of damage in the DNA.

The following events occur after DNA is subjected to radiation. The events are listed in no specific order.

W: Mutation
X: Change in cell activity
Y: Change in protein structure
Z: Change in polypeptide sequence

What is the correct sequence of steps?
questions.answer: Radiation changes the DNA base sequence (W, mutation), which changes the codons and therefore the amino acid sequence (Z, polypeptide), which changes how the protein folds (Y, protein structure), which changes what the protein does in the cell (X, cell activity): W, Z, Y, X.

questions.question:
A comet assay is a technique used to determine the amount of double-strand breakages in DNA in cells. The DNA of a nucleus placed on an agarose gel is subjected to electrophoresis and stained. Undamaged DNA appears as a round shape (the head), and fragments of damaged DNA with double-strand breaks extend out from the head (the tail), moving towards the positive terminal. The length of the tail corresponds to the amount of damage in the DNA.

In a separate experiment, cells are treated with a chemical mutagen that causes only nucleotide substitutions in DNA. Which of the following is the most correct prediction for the result of a comet assay for this treatment?
options: The tail will be longer than a cell with double-stranded breaks in DNA.
The head will remain in place and the tail will move towards the negative terminal.
The only visible part will be the head with no tail.
There will be no visible head or tail.
questions.answer: A substitution replaces one base with another and does not break the DNA backbone, so no fragments are produced. The DNA stays intact in the head and there is no tail. (DNA fragments would in any case move towards the positive terminal because DNA is negatively charged.)

questions.question:
Two linked genes in humans have the following alleles: Gene 1: A (secretor), a (non-secretor); Gene 2: B (production of protein X), b (no protein X produced). Four chromosome compositions (types) were found in a family: Type 1 = AB / ab, Type 2 = Ab / ab, Type 3 = aB / ab, Type 4 = ab / ab. The pedigree below shows the phenotypes of the family members (square = male, circle = female; the key shows how each half-shading is interpreted).

Which of the following is correct about the genotype of the identified individual?
questions.answer: Individual III-2 is a non-secretor (left half unshaded) who produces protein X (right half shaded), so is *aa* with at least one *B*, which is the type 3 composition (aB/ab). I-1 (a circle with no shading) is a non-secretor with no protein X, so is type 4, not type 1. II-2 is a secretor who produces protein X, so is not type 2 (Ab/ab makes no protein X). III-12 is a secretor with no protein X, which cannot be type 4 (ab/ab).

questions.question:
Two linked genes in humans have the following alleles: Gene 1: A (secretor), a (non-secretor); Gene 2: B (production of protein X), b (no protein X produced). Four chromosome compositions (types) were found in a family: Type 1 = AB / ab, Type 2 = Ab / ab, Type 3 = aB / ab, Type 4 = ab / ab. The pedigree is shown below.

The distance between the two genes on the chromosome can be estimated from the percentage of recombinant gametes formed following crossing over between the two genes during meiosis. Based on the pedigree presented, which of the following is the best estimate of the percentage of gametes that are formed due to crossing over between the two genes?
questions.answer:
Only matings between a double heterozygote (type 1) and a double homozygous recessive (type 4) show clearly whether the type 1 parent's gametes were recombinant. A type 1 gamete is either AB or ab (non-recombinant); type 2 (Ab) or type 3 (aB) offspring come from recombinant gametes.

- I-1 × I-2: 3 children, 1 recombinant (type 2).
- II-1 × II-2: 6 children, 1 recombinant (type 3).
- II-3 × II-4: 5 children, none recombinant.
- II-5 × II-6 give no information (all children are *bb*).

Recombinant gametes $=\dfrac{2}{3+6+5}=\dfrac{2}{14}\approx14\%$.

questions.question:
The figure represents an individual's karyotype (chromosomes arranged in numbered pairs 1–22 in groups A–G, plus the sex chromosomes X and Y; the pair at 21 has three chromosomes).

With reference to the diagram, describe the information that can be obtained from a karyotype.
questions.answer: A karyotype displays all of an individual's chromosomes, arranged in homologous pairs by size and banding. It shows the sex chromosomes, so the sex of the individual can be determined: this individual has an X and a Y chromosome and is male. It also shows chromosomal mutations or abnormalities in number or structure (such as deletions or insertions): this individual has three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), so can be diagnosed with Down syndrome.

questions.question:
Safflower is a minor crop grown in Australia, and the first commercial GM (genetically modified) safflower was released in Australia in 2018.

Describe the benefits of ONE other named transgenic crop to agriculture.
questions.answer: Bt cotton is cotton into which a gene from the soil bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* has been inserted, so the plant makes a toxin that kills the caterpillars (such as bollworm) that eat it. This reduces crop losses from pests, so yields rise, and farmers need to spray much less insecticide, which saves them money and reduces environmental damage to non-target species and to farm workers.

questions.question:
Safflower is a minor crop grown in Australia, and the first commercial GM (genetically modified) safflower was released in Australia in 2018.

Discuss ONE social or cultural issue which has influenced the use of a named GM crop.
questions.answer: A social issue that has influenced the use of herbicide-resistant (Roundup Ready) corn is public concern about the safety of GM food. Many consumers are worried that eating GM food could harm their health or that it is 'unnatural', even though scientific studies have not found GM foods approved for sale to be less safe than conventional foods. Public opposition has led some countries to ban or restrict the growing of GM corn, some supermarkets and food companies to label products or market 'non-GM' food, and some farmers to avoid growing it for fear of losing sales. On the other hand, supporters argue that GM corn produces higher yields, so it helps feed a growing population, so the issue is a balance between perceived risk and the benefit to food supply. (Cultural views, such as religious or traditional objections to altering organisms, have also influenced acceptance.)

questions.question:
The Amur leopard, *Panthera pardus orientalis*, is a subspecies of leopard found only in Russia and China. It is listed as Critically Endangered with an estimated population of 100 individuals recorded in 2017. Breeding programs are used in zoological parks to help avoid extinction.

The gel electrophoresis shown considers several DNA markers for a female Amur leopard (F) and three potential mates (M1, M2, M3) from other zoos (S is the standard).

Justify the use of gel electrophoresis in selecting the pair of Amur leopards, from this captive population, that you would recommend for breeding. Support your answer with reference to the data.
questions.answer:
Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size, so each animal's DNA profile shows how many fragments (markers) it shares with another animal. This is a measure of how closely related they are. In a very small, endangered population, breeding between closely related animals (inbreeding) reduces genetic diversity and increases the chance of offspring being homozygous for harmful recessive alleles, so the best pair to breed is the one with the greatest difference between their profiles.

From the gel, male M1 shares two bands with the female F, male M3 shares three bands with F, but male M2 shares only one band. I would recommend F and M2 as the breeding pair, since M2 is the least related to F, so their offspring will have the highest genetic diversity. This will help maintain the gene pool of the captive population and give it the best chance of surviving and adapting.

*Note:* the school's marking table shows 5 marks; the paper states 4.

questions.question:
Giardiasis is the most common form of non-bacterial diarrhoea in people in Australia. The adult parasite, *Giardia lamblia*, is a single cell that lives in the upper part of the intestine (duodenum) of an infected person, where it rapidly multiplies. To pass from one human to another it encloses itself in a cyst that passes out in the faeces.

Describe ONE procedure that would be suitable for preventing the spread of Giardia and justify its use.
questions.answer: Procedure: washing hands thoroughly with soap and water after going to the toilet (and before preparing or eating food), together with safe disposal of faeces. Justification: Giardia is spread by the faecal–oral route, when cysts in the faeces of an infected person are transferred on hands, food or water to the mouth of another person. Handwashing with soap physically removes and washes away the cysts from the hands, so they cannot be passed on to food, surfaces or other people. This breaks the chain of transmission, is cheap, easy and effective, and can be carried out by everyone, including in communities with limited resources.

questions.question:
Some types of leukocytes can change their shape to engulf foreign particles, for example bacteria. This process also includes the foreign particle being destroyed inside the cell.

Name the process described above.
questions.answer: Phagocytosis.

questions.question:
Phagocytosis is a non-specific response to an antigen.

Outline ONE physical change that occurs in a host's cell or tissue in response to a pathogen by the human immune system.
questions.answer: Inflammation: when tissue is damaged or infected, the blood vessels near the site dilate and become more permeable, so more blood and fluid flow into the area. This causes visible physical changes such as redness, heat and swelling of the tissue, and allows phagocytes to move out of the capillaries into the tissue to engulf the pathogens.

questions.question:
The graph shows the change in antibody concentration over time after vaccination involving an initial and then a second, or booster, dose.

Identify the time at which the primary and secondary vaccinations were given and account for the features of the graph using your knowledge of primary and secondary immune response. Annotate the graph to support your answer.
questions.answer:
The primary vaccination was given at the start of the graph (time 0, where the curve begins to rise). The booster (secondary vaccination) was given at the lowest point between the two peaks, just before the second curve rises sharply.

Primary response: the first exposure to the antigen activates only a few B lymphocytes with matching receptors, with the help of T helper cells. They must be selected, clone and differentiate into plasma cells, so there is a lag before antibodies appear, the antibody concentration rises slowly to a low peak and then falls as the antibodies are used up or broken down and the plasma cells die. Some of the activated B cells (and T cells) become long-lived memory cells.

Secondary response: when the same antigen is met again, the memory cells recognise it quickly and respond immediately, so there is a very short lag. There are many more memory cells than there were naïve B cells, which divide rapidly into large numbers of plasma cells, so the antibody concentration rises faster, reaches a much higher peak and stays higher for longer, falling back to a higher baseline than after the primary response. More antibody remaining in the blood gives longer protection against the pathogen.

questions.question:
Sexual reproduction is a mechanism that has evolved to ensure the continuity of species. In animals several reproductive strategies ensure that reproduction occurs effectively in the environment they live in. Both internal and external fertilisation strategies are known to produce reproductive success.

"Internal fertilisation is more advantageous than external fertilisation in ensuring the continuity of a species."

Assess the above statement.
questions.answer:
Internal fertilisation (e.g. in mammals and reptiles) has clear advantages: the gametes are placed directly together inside the female's body, so the chance of fertilisation is high and fewer gametes need to be made. The embryo is protected from predators, desiccation and temperature changes (in the uterus or within a shelled egg), and survival is further improved by parental care, so far fewer offspring are needed. Its disadvantages are that it requires mating (a partner must be found), the energy cost of pregnancy or egg formation and parental care is high, and fewer offspring are produced per breeding season.

External fertilisation (e.g. in fish and frogs) is also successful: it needs no mating contact and enormous numbers of gametes are released into water, and this variation helps species survive. However, it requires a moist or aquatic environment to prevent the gametes drying out, and eggs and larvae are exposed to predation, so survival of offspring is low and the large number of gametes must be produced to compensate.

Overall, the statement is largely supported: internal fertilisation gives a higher survival rate per offspring and allows animals to live in a wider range of habitats, including on land. But it is not the only successful strategy, since external fertilisation also ensures continuity of species in the aquatic environments to which they are adapted, so the statement is true only in the sense of being 'more advantageous' under many terrestrial conditions, not essential.

questions.question:
Lead poisoning is a serious health problem. Too much lead can affect all organs, including the kidneys, causing 'lead-related nephrotoxicity'. In extreme cases nephrotoxicity causes polycystic kidney disease, in which fluid-filled cysts grow in the kidney, interfering with the normal kidney tissue and limiting the kidney's ability to filter the blood. The number of cysts builds up over time, enlarging the kidney and ultimately causing renal failure.

Evaluate the effectiveness of an identified technology that can assist with this type of disorder. In your answer include any specific limitations of the treatment or consequences for the patient's diet and/or lifestyle associated with the use of this technology.
questions.answer:
Technology: haemodialysis. Blood is pumped out of the body, through a dialysis machine in which it flows past a partially permeable membrane with dialysate flowing in the opposite direction. Wastes such as urea and excess salts and water diffuse or are filtered out, and the cleaned blood is returned to the body, so it does the filtering that the failed kidneys can no longer do.

Effectiveness: it is effective at keeping patients alive, removing waste products, correcting the salt and water balance and controlling blood pressure, so it manages kidney failure when there is no kidney available for transplant, but it does not cure the disease, and it cannot do the hormonal functions of the kidney (e.g. making erythropoietin), so patients can develop anaemia.

Limitations and consequences: treatment takes about 4 hours, 3 times each week at a hospital or dialysis centre (or at home), which restricts work and travel; there is a risk of infection at the access site and of low blood pressure and fatigue; and it is expensive. Patients must restrict their intake of fluids, salt, potassium and phosphorus (and often protein), so their diet is restricted. Many patients therefore will hope for a kidney transplant, which allows a more normal lifestyle but requires lifelong immunosuppressant drugs.

questions.question:
The coiled-coil was one of the earliest tertiary protein structures described and was first discovered in the two-stranded coiled-coil protein alpha-keratin. Coiled-coils consist of two or more alpha-helices winding around each other. Such proteins are involved in a wide variety of structural and mechanical processes in cells.

Long-CC (LCC) includes long coiled-coils with a minimum stretch of 70 amino acids in one coiled coil and a minimum stretch of 50 amino acids in the other.

A study compared the presence of CC and LCC proteins in species from different kingdoms. The graph shows the estimated percentages of CC proteins, LCC proteins and superlong CC per genome for 22 different species (A: Archaea; B: Gram-positive bacteria; C: Gram-negative bacteria; D: Fungi; E: Animals; F: Plants).

"Animals are more closely related to plants than other kingdoms."

Analyse the data provided and assess whether this statement is supported.
questions.answer:
Reading the graph, the percentage of coiled-coil proteins per genome is about 2–4% in Archaea (2.0–3.0%), 2–4% in Gram-positive bacteria (about 1.8–4.3%) and 2–6% in Gram-negative bacteria (about 2.4–5.6%). Fungi (about 5.6–6.0%), plants (about 5.6–6.7%) and animals (about 5.4–8.3%) all have higher percentages, around 5–8%. Long coiled-coils follow the same pattern: roughly 0.3–1% of the genome in the prokaryotes but about 1–3% in fungi, plants and animals.

The data partly support the statement: animals and plants have similar, high percentages of coiled-coil proteins which are clearly higher than the prokaryotes (Archaea and bacteria), suggesting that they share a more recent common ancestor with each other than with the prokaryotes. However, fungi are just as similar to plants and animals as they are to each other (and animals have the highest values), so the data do not show that animals are more closely related to plants than to fungi; indeed, other evidence shows that animals are more closely related to fungi. The data are also limited: only 22 species are included, with only 2 plants and 2 fungi, and the proportion of coiled-coil proteins is a single feature, so the conclusion that animals are more closely related to plants than to other kingdoms is not clearly supported without further genetic evidence.

questions.question:
The data below examines the changes in allele frequencies at a single locus with two alleles, B and b, in two very large populations of rabbits (x and y) due to natural selection. The furless rabbit is rarely found in the wild because the cold English winters are a selective pressure against it. The dominant allele for normal fur is represented by B and the recessive allele for no fur is represented by b.

| Generation | Frequency of b, Population x | Frequency of b, Population y |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| 10 | 0.37 | 0.65 |
| 20 | 0.30 | 0.80 |
| 30 | 0.24 | 0.90 |
| 40 | 0.20 | 0.98 |
| 50 | 0.18 | 1.00 |
| 60 | 0.14 | 1.00 |
| 70 | 0.12 | 1.00 |
| 80 | 0.12 | 1.00 |
| 90 | 0.10 | 1.00 |
| 100 | 0.10 | 1.00 |

Graph the frequencies of B and b as a function of generation.
questions.answer: Plot generation (0–100) on the horizontal axis and allele frequency (0–1.0) on the vertical axis, for each population draw one line for *b* (given) and one for *B*, where $f(B)=1-f(b)$ since the two frequencies must add to 1. Label the axes and the lines (see graph). In population x, *b* falls from 0.50 to 0.10 and *B* rises from 0.50 to 0.90; in population y, *b* rises from 0.50 to 1.00 (reaching 1.0 by generation 50) and *B* falls from 0.50 to 0.

questions.question:
Frequencies of the alleles B (dominant, normal fur) and b (recessive, furless) in two very large rabbit populations were followed over 100 generations. In population x, the frequency of b fell from 0.50 to 0.10 and then levelled off; in population y, the frequency of b rose from 0.50 to 1.00 by generation 50 and then stayed at 1.00. The furless rabbit is rarely found in the wild because the cold English winters are a selective pressure against it.

Account for the shape of the graph. Support your answer with reference to the information provided.
questions.answer: In population x, natural selection acts against the furless phenotype (*bb*), because furless rabbits are less likely to survive cold winters and reproduce, so the frequency of *b* falls quickly at first. The decline slows and levels off at about 0.1 because the *b* allele is hidden from selection in heterozygotes (*Bb*), which have fur and so survive; only the rare *bb* are selected against, so it is eliminated very slowly. In population y the selective pressure is reversed (it favours furless rabbits, for example in a warm environment, or a different selection pressure), so *b* increases until it is fixed at 1.0 by generation 50 (all rabbits are *bb*), after which there is no variation left for selection to act on, so the frequency stays constant.

questions.question:
In rabbits, a second, unlinked gene controls the length of fur, if any. Long hair (L) is dominant over short hair (l). The dominant allele for normal fur is B and the recessive allele for no fur is b.

A long-haired rabbit was crossed with a furless rabbit to produce many offspring, all of which have fur. One-quarter of the offspring are short-haired rabbits.

Deduce the genotypes of the two parent rabbits. Show working.
questions.answer:
All the offspring have fur (*B_*) and the furless parent is *bb*, so the long-haired parent must be homozygous *BB* (if it were *Bb*, half of the offspring would be furless). One quarter of the offspring are short-haired (*ll*), so each parent must carry an *l* allele: the long-haired parent is heterozygous *Ll* and the furless rabbit (whose hair length gene cannot be seen) must also be *Ll* (a cross *Ll* × *ll* would give half short, and *Ll* × *LL* none).

Parent genotypes: long-haired rabbit *BBLl*; furless rabbit *bbLl*.

Punnett square for the length of hair gene (*Ll* × *Ll*):

| | L | l |
|---|---|---|
| **L** | LL | Ll |
| **l** | Ll | ll |

The ratio is 3 long : 1 short, and all offspring are *Bb* so all have fur, matching the data.

questions.question:
Foetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs) are one of a growing class of lifestyle-caused disorders. FASDs are a group of conditions that can occur in a person whose mother drank alcohol during pregnancy. People with FAS have central nervous system (CNS) problems, minor facial feature abnormalities and growth problems, and can have problems with learning, memory, attention span, communication, vision or hearing. They often have a hard time in school and trouble getting along with others.

The poster shows an example from an educational program that targets FASD (International Foetal Alcohol Syndrome Awareness Day: 'Drinking alcohol during pregnancy can cause lifelong harm to the unborn child').

Explain the use of this educational program to society.
questions.answer: FASD is caused entirely by a lifestyle choice (drinking alcohol during pregnancy) and so is completely preventable. Educational programs and posters like this one inform women who are pregnant, or planning to become pregnant, (and their partners and families) that drinking alcohol can cause permanent harm to the unborn child, so they can choose not to drink. This reduces the incidence of FASD, so fewer children are born with lifelong disabilities, which improves quality of life for these children and their families. It also reduces the cost to society of health care, special education and disability support, and raises awareness among health professionals and the community, so that everyone shares the responsibility for supporting pregnant women to avoid alcohol.

questions.question:
*Agrobacterium tumefaciens* is a rod-shaped bacterium found in soil. Its flagella allow it to move through the soil in response to chemicals released by wounded plant cells. Once it enters its plant host, it injects a section of its DNA called the T-DNA, derived from its Ti (tumour-inducing) plasmid, into its host, causing the host to form undifferentiated (tumour) tissue termed a crown gall.

Compare the forms in which DNA is found in agrobacterium and its host plant before infection.
questions.answer: Similarities: both have DNA that is double-stranded and associated with proteins; both have circular DNA (the bacterium's chromosome and its Ti plasmid, and the plant's chloroplast and mitochondrial DNA). Differences: the DNA of the plant's nucleus is in several linear chromosomes, wrapped around histone proteins and enclosed in a nuclear membrane, whereas agrobacterium has a single, circular chromosome (plus plasmids), lying free in the cytoplasm with no nucleus and not wound around histones.

questions.question:
*Agrobacterium tumefaciens* is a rod-shaped bacterium found in soil. Its flagella allow it to move through the soil in response to chemicals released by wounded plant cells. Once it enters its plant host, it injects a section of its DNA called the T-DNA, derived from its Ti (tumour-inducing) plasmid, into its host, causing the host to form undifferentiated (tumour) tissue termed a crown gall.

Explain how agrobacterium can operate as a mutagen.
questions.answer: Agrobacterium injects its T-DNA into the plant cell, where it is integrated into the plant's genome. This inserts extra bases (genes) into the plant DNA, which changes its base sequence (an insertion mutation) and so changes how the genes work. The T-DNA genes produce enzymes that make auxin and cytokinin, causing uncontrolled cell division and the growth of a tumour. Because the plant DNA has been permanently changed, agrobacterium acts as a mutagen.

questions.question:
Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a soil bacterium that injects T-DNA from its Ti plasmid into plants, causing a crown gall (tumour). Information on the interaction between a plant and Agrobacterium:

(A) Agrobacteria cells produce the hormones cytokinin and auxin, which increase host susceptibility and inhibit H₂O₂ production and the hypersensitive response (HR) upon infection.
(B) After integration of the bacterial T-DNA into the plant genome, cytokinin and auxin are synthesised by T-DNA-encoded enzymes and accumulate inside the tumour.
(C) This causes massive changes in the gene expression pattern, resulting in metabolomic and morphological adaptations that are necessary for tumour growth and differentiation.
(D) Loss of water is minimised by an increase in the levels of the stress hormone ABA. Evaporation of water from the disrupted crown gall surface drives the flow of water and minerals into crown galls.
(E) Because photosynthesis is downregulated, the O₂ levels are low; the tumour produces C and N compounds heterotrophically and gains energy mainly anaerobically by alcoholic fermentation.
(F) The developing tumour becomes a metabolic sink for the host plant, which accumulates metabolites produced by source leaves and minerals taken up by the roots.
(G) Auxin and cytokinin also cause an increase in ethylene (ET) which together with salicylic acid (SA) inhibits agrobacterial virulence.
(H) ABA induces DNA methylation of the plant genome, regulating gene expression of drought-stress responsive genes. The oncogenes of the T-DNA remain unaffected by methylation of the plant genome.

Outline ONE response of the plant to agrobacterium infection.
questions.answer: Auxin and cytokinin produced in the infected tissue cause the plant to increase its production of ethylene, which together with salicylic acid inhibits the virulence of the agrobacteria. This is a chemical defence response that limits the infection. (Alternatively: the plant increases ABA to reduce water loss from the disrupted gall surface.)

Describe ONE adaptation that makes agrobacterium a successful pathogen of plants.
questions.answer: Agrobacterium has flagella, which it uses to swim through the soil towards chemicals released by wounded plant cells, so it can find and enter a suitable host through wounds. (Alternatively: it injects T-DNA that causes the plant to produce hormones that make the host more susceptible and suppress its defences (hypersensitive response), allowing the bacteria to colonise it.)

Identify a mechanism by which the plant maintains homeostasis when infected by agrobacterium.
questions.answer: The plant increases the level of the hormone abscisic acid (ABA), which minimises water loss from the disrupted gall surface and so helps to maintain the plant's water balance.

(H) ABA induces DNA methylation of the plant genome, regulating gene expression of drought-stress responsive genes. The oncogenes of the T-DNA remain unaffected by methylation of the plant genome.

"Regulation of genes affects the phenotype of the organism."

Discuss this statement using the information provided.
questions.answer: The information supports the statement. Once the T-DNA is integrated, the genes for making auxin and cytokinin are expressed, and these hormones cause massive changes in the pattern of gene expression (C), turning some genes on and others off. These changes in expression change the plant's phenotype: the cells stay undifferentiated and divide rapidly to form a tumour (crown gall). Gene expression is also changed by the downregulation of photosynthesis genes, so the tumour has low oxygen and the plant's metabolism changes (the tumour gains energy by fermentation and becomes a metabolic sink), which can stunt the growth of the plant. In (H), ABA causes methylation of the plant DNA, which regulates drought-response genes, so water loss is limited. Methylation of the T-DNA oncogenes does not occur, so they remain active and the tumour keeps growing. So regulation of gene expression, by both the bacterium and the plant, changes the structure, metabolism and behaviour of the plant.

questions.question:
Rubella is an infectious disease caused by *Rubivirus rubella*. The disease is frequently mild, with a characteristic rash often appearing two weeks after exposure and lasting three days. Rubella is usually spread from one person to the next through the air via coughs of people who are infected. Once recovered, people are immune to future infections. In the early 1940s Australian ophthalmologist Norman Gregg noticed a high incidence of congenital cataracts in babies whose mothers had suffered from rubella during pregnancy. Infection during early pregnancy may result in a miscarriage or a child born with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). The main defects result almost exclusively from rubella infection in the first 16 weeks of gestation and include deafness due to cochlea malformation, eye and cardiovascular defects, and central nervous system damage leading to mental retardation.

Rubella is preventable with a single dose of the rubella vaccine, which is more than 95% effective. When rubella vaccination became feasible around 1971, both the United States and the United Kingdom began vaccination programs. In the United States the strategy was to vaccinate infants, so that eventually the reservoir in childhood would be abolished. In contrast, the United Kingdom decided on a program of vaccinating adolescent girls. Both strategies were partial successes, in that CRS incidence began to decrease.

Figure 1 (graph) shows the number of rubella cases (dashed line, left axis, 0–70 000) and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) cases (solid line, right axis, 0–100) in the United States, 1966–2011.

Describe the trends in the incidence of infectious rubella cases.
questions.answer: The number of rubella cases was very high in the late 1960s (about 47 000 cases per year in 1966, peaking at about 57 000 around 1969), then fell steeply to about 12 000–20 000 per year in the mid-1970s, under 5000 per year by 1981, under 1000 per year after about 1985, with almost no cases after 1992. There were smaller peaks (outbreaks) of about 17 000–20 000 cases in about 1975 and 1977–78, and only very small ones (about 1000 cases) around 1991, each far smaller than the one before, so the overall trend is a large decline following vaccination.

Figure 1 (graph) shows the number of rubella cases (dashed line, left axis, 0–70 000) and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) cases (solid line, right axis, 0–100) in the United States, 1966–2011.

Use the evidence in the graph to justify the statement that the US program was only a partial success in reducing the rate of CRS.
questions.answer: The US program was a success in that CRS cases fell from about 90 per year in 1970 to nearly none (0–2) from the late 1990s, and rubella cases fell from about 57 000 to under 1000 per year. But it was only a partial success because CRS did not fall in step with rubella: CRS cases rose again to about 60 around 1980 and to about 40 in 1991 (and about 15 around 1986), even though rubella cases had fallen to a few thousand or fewer, so some babies were still being born with CRS for many years after the program began.

In contrast, the United Kingdom decided on a program of vaccinating adolescent girls. Both strategies were partial successes, in that CRS incidence began to decrease.

Justify a hypothesis as to why the UK program (vaccinating adolescent girls only) was only a partial success in reducing the rate of CRS.
questions.answer: Hypothesis: the UK program was only a partial success because rubella continued to circulate in the community, mainly in boys and in girls who had not yet been vaccinated. Justification: only adolescent girls were vaccinated, so boys and younger children remained susceptible and were a reservoir of the virus. They could continue to catch and pass on rubella, and pregnant women who had not been vaccinated (for example, those too old for the program or who missed the vaccine) were still exposed to it. With no herd immunity, CRS cases did not fall as much as in the US, where all infants were vaccinated and virus transmission was interrupted.

In the United States the strategy was to vaccinate infants, so that eventually the reservoir in childhood would be abolished. In contrast, the United Kingdom decided on a program of vaccinating adolescent girls. Both strategies were partial successes, in that CRS incidence began to decrease.

Today, most developed countries have a comprehensive immunisation program and rubella has been eliminated in many areas of the world. However, in a number of developing countries rubella infections are common and a significant number of babies are born with CRS. (Figure 2 is a world map of the estimated median number of CRS cases born by country in 2010: highest in South Asia, central Africa and parts of South-East Asia, fewest in developed countries.)

Explain how a named medical technology could be used to treat a symptom of CRS and propose a reason why this is not routinely done.
questions.answer: A cochlear implant could be used to treat deafness caused by a malformed cochlea. A microphone picks up sound and a speech processor converts it to electrical signals; these are sent to an electrode array surgically inserted into the cochlea, which stimulates the auditory nerve directly, bypassing the damaged hair cells, so the brain can interpret the signals as sound. It is not routinely done because most CRS cases now occur in developing countries (see the map), where the implants and the surgery, and the specialist follow-up such as hearing and speech therapy, are too expensive and not available to most families. (Alternatively: surgical lens replacement for cataracts.)

The mechanism for how CRS occurs is not clear, although it is known that the pathogen crosses the placenta and infects the embryo. It appears that the rate of mitosis in some embryonic tissues is decreased.

Explain how a reduced rate of mitosis could cause ONE identified symptom of CRS.
questions.answer: Mitosis produces the new cells needed for growth of the embryo. If the rate of mitosis is reduced in the developing ear, fewer cells are produced, so the cochlea cannot grow to its full size or form properly at the critical stages of embryonic development (the first 16 weeks), and it is malformed. Because the cochlea is malformed, the hair cells cannot detect sound properly, and the baby is deaf. (Similarly, fewer cells in the developing lens or heart would cause cataracts or heart defects.)

When rubella vaccination became feasible around 1971, both the United States and the United Kingdom began vaccination programs. In the United States the strategy was to vaccinate infants, so that eventually the reservoir in childhood would be abolished. In contrast, the United Kingdom decided on a program of vaccinating adolescent girls. Both strategies were partial successes, in that CRS incidence began to decrease.

An alternative hypothesis for the mechanism is that some of the symptoms of CRS are due to maternal infection causing malfunction of the mother's liver, resulting in excessively high (toxic) levels of vitamin A in the blood of both the mother and the developing embryo. Vitamin A is stored in the liver and is also found in the diet in cheese, dairy, liver and meat.

A group of unvaccinated pregnant women in a developing region has just been exposed to rubella virus.

Outline an epidemiological study that could be carried out ethically to test the vitamin A hypothesis. In your answer, state the type of study, describe the method and describe what results would support the hypothesis.
questions.answer:
Type of study: a prospective, analytic, experimental study (a controlled, blind cohort study).

Method: select pregnant women who are in the first 16 weeks of pregnancy (dated by ultrasound) and who have been exposed to rubella and are confirmed to be infected (by blood test or symptoms), after giving informed consent. Randomly allocate them to two groups: a control group who eat their normal diet, and an experimental group whose diet is modified to be low in vitamin A (still adequate for health, so that it is not harmful to the mother or the baby, for ethical reasons; no one is given extra vitamin A, which could harm the baby). Measure the vitamin A level in the blood of the women regularly and monitor the pregnancies, and after birth examine all the babies for signs of CRS (e.g. deafness, cataracts, heart defects). All the women receive the same standard medical care, the examiners should not know which group each baby belongs to (blind), and a large sample is used to reduce the effect of chance.

Results supporting the hypothesis: if the women with lower blood vitamin A levels (the experimental group) have fewer babies born with CRS symptoms than the control group, and there is a positive correlation between the level of vitamin A in the blood and the number of CRS defects, the vitamin A hypothesis would be supported.

*Note:* the original paper provides a table to circle the type of study and fill in the method and results, which has been rewritten as a single question.

questions.question:
Evaluate the importance of validity in biological research.

In your response, refer to:

- a study of your own design, such as an epidemiological study investigating whether a hypothesis (for example, that CRS symptoms are caused by toxic levels of vitamin A) is correct, in which unvaccinated pregnant women exposed to rubella are followed,
- ONE other named epidemiological study that you have investigated as part of your course,
- ONE first-hand investigation that you have carried out as part of your course, and
- ONE second-hand investigation that you have carried out as part of your course.
questions.answer:
Validity is the extent to which an investigation measures what it claims to measure and answers the question it set out to test. It is important because a result from an invalid investigation, however precise, cannot be relied on, so the conclusions drawn (and any decisions made from them, such as health policy) may be wrong. An investigation is valid if only the independent variable is changed, all other variables are controlled, an appropriate control group is used, measurements are accurate and suited to the question, and the sample is large and representative.

**The vitamin A study:** the study would be valid if it measured blood vitamin A (the independent variable) and CRS defects in the babies (the dependent variable), with women randomly allocated to groups, matched in age, gestation and infection, with a control group, a large sample and examiners who did not know which group the babies came from. If women differed in other ways (e.g. nutrition, or the virus strain) that affect CRS, the study would not be valid, because the effect could not be attributed to vitamin A.

**A named epidemiological study** (e.g. the British Doctors Study on smoking and lung cancer): the study followed about 34 000 doctors for 50 years and compared smokers and non-smokers, with deaths and smoking habits recorded and other factors considered, so its conclusion that smoking causes lung cancer was valid, and led to public-health action. Its validity was supported by the large sample, long follow-up and the presence of a dose–response relationship, although the study was observational and the doctors were not a perfectly representative group.

**A first-hand investigation** (e.g. a practical on the effect of a disinfectant or antibiotic on bacterial growth using agar plates): the validity depended on using a control (a disc with water), the same volume and concentration, the same type of bacteria, incubation time and temperature, sterile technique, measuring the zone of inhibition accurately and repeating the trials. If these were not controlled, any differences in the zones of inhibition might be due to other factors and not to the disinfectant.

**A second-hand investigation** (e.g. an article on a plant's response to a pathogen, or a data set on disease incidence): the validity of the source was judged by whether the study used controls and a large, representative sample, whether it was peer-reviewed and published by a reputable source, whether the data support the conclusion and whether other studies agree.

Therefore, validity makes it possible to trust the conclusions of an investigation, and all the studies discussed show that validity is achieved by controlling variables, using a control, large samples and appropriate measurement. Without it, reliability and accuracy do not matter, since the investigation would not test what it was meant to. (This answer depends on the student's own named investigations; the school's sample refers to its own course investigations, such as testing microbes in water and a plant–pathogen article.)
